lines.text: Americans owe more on student loans than on credit cards.
lines.say: Americans owe more on student loans than on credit cards.

lines.text: As of September 2026, student debt stood at $1.66 trillion. Credit cards? $1.29 trillion.
lines.say: As of September twenty twenty-six, student debt stood at one point six six trillion dollars. Credit cards? One point two nine trillion.

lines.text: That's New York Fed data. Among household debts, only mortgages and auto loans are bigger.
lines.say: That's New York Fed data. Among household debts, only mortgages and auto loans are bigger.

lines.text: Federal data counts 42.3 million people with federal student loans, as of June 2026.
lines.say: Federal data counts forty-two point three million people with federal student loans, as of June twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: They owe more than $1.7 trillion. Our math: that's over $40,000 each, on average.
lines.say: They owe more than one point seven trillion dollars. Our math: that's over forty thousand dollars each, on average.

lines.text: So how did a program meant to open college doors turn into a pile this big?
lines.say: So how did a program meant to open college doors turn into a pile this big?

lines.text: The answer is four things stacked together: who lends, rising prices, easier borrowing, and interest that never sleeps.
lines.say: The answer is four things stacked together: who lends, rising prices, easier borrowing, and interest that never sleeps.

lines.text: Quick note: this is news and education, not financial advice, and it takes no political side.
lines.say: Quick note: this is news and education, not financial advice, and it takes no political side.

lines.text: Chapter one: where the loans came from.
lines.say: Chapter one: where the loans came from.

lines.text: In 1958, a Cold War law, the National Defense Education Act, created the first federal student loans.
lines.say: In nineteen fifty-eight, a Cold War law, the National Defense Education Act, created the first federal student loans.

lines.text: Then, on November 8, 1965, President Lyndon Johnson signed the Higher Education Act.
lines.say: Then, on November eighth, nineteen sixty-five, President Lyndon Johnson signed the Higher Education Act.

lines.text: His goal: any high school senior could apply to college and, in his words, "not be turned away because his family is poor."
lines.say: His goal: any high school senior could apply to college and, in his words, not be turned away because his family is poor.

scene.text: ...and not be turned away because his family is poor.

lines.text: The law created Guaranteed Student Loans. Banks lent the money, and the government promised to cover it if students didn't pay.
lines.say: The law created Guaranteed Student Loans. Banks lent the money, and the government promised to cover it if students didn't pay.

lines.text: For banks, that was a low-risk setup: they earned the interest, and the government carried most of the risk.
lines.say: For banks, that was a low-risk setup: they earned the interest, and the government carried most of the risk.

lines.text: Back to the timeline. In 1976, Congress made federal student loans much harder to wipe out in bankruptcy.
lines.say: Back to the timeline. In nineteen seventy-six, Congress made federal student loans much harder to wipe out in bankruptcy.

lines.text: Borrowers had to prove "undue hardship" in the early years of repayment. In 1998, that time limit was removed entirely.
lines.say: Borrowers had to prove undue hardship in the early years of repayment. In nineteen ninety-eight, that time limit was removed entirely.

lines.text: And in 2005, a big bankruptcy law extended the same tough rule to private student loans from banks.
lines.say: And in two thousand five, a big bankruptcy law extended the same tough rule to private student loans from banks.

lines.text: Here's why that matters. Credit card debt can often be wiped out in bankruptcy, but student loans usually stick around.
lines.say: Here's why that matters. Credit card debt can often be wiped out in bankruptcy, but student loans usually stick around.

lines.text: So for lenders, student loans became unusually safe. And for borrowers, unusually sticky.
lines.say: So for lenders, student loans became unusually safe. And for borrowers, unusually sticky.

lines.text: Chapter two: the price went up.
lines.say: Chapter two: the price went up.

lines.text: For the 2026-27 school year, College Board puts average published tuition and fees at a public four-year college, in-state, at $12,290.
lines.say: For the twenty twenty-six to twenty-seven school year, College Board puts average published tuition and fees at a public four-year college, in-state, at twelve thousand two hundred ninety dollars.

lines.text: That's the sticker price, before grants and scholarships knock it down for many students. Housing and food come on top.
lines.say: That's the sticker price, before grants and scholarships knock it down for many students. Housing and food come on top.

lines.text: For the long view, College Board's 2025 report uses 2025 dollars, so inflation is already taken out. In 1995-96, it was $5,940.
lines.say: For the long view, College Board's twenty twenty-five report uses twenty twenty-five dollars, so inflation is already taken out. In nineteen ninety-five to ninety-six, it was five thousand nine hundred forty dollars.

lines.text: By 2015-16, it had climbed to a peak of about $12,810. By 2025-26, it was $11,950.
lines.say: By twenty fifteen to sixteen, it had climbed to a peak of about twelve thousand eight hundred ten dollars. By twenty twenty-five to twenty-six, it was eleven thousand nine hundred fifty.

lines.text: Our math: after inflation, the sticker price at a public four-year college about doubled in thirty years.
lines.say: Our math: after inflation, the sticker price at a public four-year college about doubled in thirty years.

lines.text: In plain numbers, that's $6,010 more per year, in 2025 dollars, for the exact same seat in class.
lines.say: In plain numbers, that's six thousand ten dollars more per year, in twenty twenty-five dollars, for the exact same seat in class.

lines.text: Researchers still argue about why. Some point to state funding cuts, some to campus spending, and some to easy federal loans.
lines.say: Researchers still argue about why. Some point to state funding cuts, some to campus spending, and some to easy federal loans.

lines.text: But here's the twist. College Board says that sticker price fell 7% after inflation in the ten years through 2025-26.
lines.say: But here's the twist. College Board says that sticker price fell seven percent after inflation in the ten years through twenty twenty-five to twenty-six.

lines.text: That's a drop of $860 in real terms. Its newest report shows an 8% real drop in the ten years through 2026-27.
lines.say: That's a drop of eight hundred sixty dollars in real terms. Its newest report shows an eight percent real drop in the ten years through twenty twenty-six to twenty-seven.

lines.text: But by then, the debt pile had already been built, and interest was keeping it there.
lines.say: But by then, the debt pile had already been built, and interest was keeping it there.

lines.text: Chapter three: the borrowing boom.
lines.say: Chapter three: the borrowing boom.

lines.text: By the end of 2012, the New York Fed said student loans had become the biggest household debt after mortgages.
lines.say: By the end of twenty twelve, the New York Fed said student loans had become the biggest household debt after mortgages.

lines.text: Here's the New York Fed's count at the end of every other year. At the end of 2012, it was $966 billion, just under a trillion.
lines.say: Here's the New York Fed's count at the end of every other year. At the end of twenty twelve, it was nine hundred sixty-six billion dollars, just under a trillion.

lines.text: Then it climbed by about $600 billion in eight years, to $1.56 trillion by the end of 2020. That's our math.
lines.say: Then it climbed by about six hundred billion dollars in eight years, to one point five six trillion by the end of twenty twenty. That's our math.

lines.text: After that, it nearly stalled: $1.62 trillion at the end of 2024, and $1.66 trillion by September 2026.
lines.say: After that, it nearly stalled: one point six two trillion at the end of twenty twenty-four, and one point six six trillion by September twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: In other words, the steep part of the climb happened before 2020. Since then, it's been close to flat.
lines.say: In other words, the steep part of the climb happened before twenty twenty. Since then, it's been close to flat.

lines.text: So what fueled the boom years? Two rule changes stand out. First, Grad PLUS loans arrived for the 2006-07 school year.
lines.say: So what fueled the boom years? Two rule changes stand out. First, Grad PLUS loans arrived for the twenty oh-six to oh-seven school year.

lines.text: Grad PLUS let graduate students borrow up to the full cost of attendance, minus other aid. No fixed dollar cap.
lines.say: Grad PLUS let graduate students borrow up to the full cost of attendance, minus other aid. No fixed dollar cap.

lines.text: Second, starting July 1, 2010, the government stopped guaranteeing bank loans and started lending directly.
lines.say: Second, starting July first, twenty ten, the government stopped guaranteeing bank loans and started lending directly.

lines.text: Since then, the lender for new federal student loans has been the US Department of Education itself.
lines.say: Since then, the lender for new federal student loans has been the US Department of Education itself.

lines.text: Supporters said it cut out bank middlemen and saved money. Critics worried it made borrowing too easy. Either way, the money kept flowing.
lines.say: Supporters said it cut out bank middlemen and saved money. Critics worried it made borrowing too easy. Either way, the money kept flowing.

lines.text: The Federal Reserve Board's broader measure tells the same story: $481 billion in March 2006, versus $1.86 trillion by June 2026.
lines.say: The Federal Reserve Board's broader measure tells the same story: four hundred eighty-one billion dollars in March two thousand six, versus one point eight six trillion by June twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Our math: that's about 3.9 times as much. It counts loans differently than the New York Fed, so the two don't mix.
lines.say: Our math: that's about three point nine times as much. It counts loans differently than the New York Fed, so the two don't mix.

lines.text: For scale, all US household debt was $19.1 trillion in Q3 2026. Student loans were about 9% of it, by our math.
lines.say: For scale, all US household debt was nineteen point one trillion dollars in the third quarter of twenty twenty-six. Student loans were about nine percent of it, by our math.

lines.text: Put it together: higher prices, easy access to loans, and years of interest. That's the recipe for the pile.
lines.say: Put it together: higher prices, easy access to loans, and years of interest. That's the recipe for the pile.

lines.text: Chapter four: what a loan really costs.
lines.say: Chapter four: what a loan really costs.

lines.text: Federal undergraduate loans made from July 2026 through June 2027 carry a fixed rate of 6.52%.
lines.say: Federal undergraduate loans made from July twenty twenty-six through June twenty twenty-seven carry a fixed rate of six point five two percent.

lines.text: That rate is set each spring from the 10-year Treasury auction, plus a fixed add-on of 2.05 percentage points.
lines.say: That rate is set each spring from the ten-year Treasury auction, plus a fixed add-on of two point oh five percentage points.

lines.text: Graduate loans cost more: 8.07% for grad students' regular loans, and 9.07% for PLUS loans.
lines.say: Graduate loans cost more: eight point oh seven percent for grad students' regular loans, and nine point oh seven percent for PLUS loans.

lines.text: So let's run one. Our math: a $30,000 undergrad loan at 6.52%, paid over the standard ten years.
lines.say: So let's run one. Our math: a thirty thousand dollar undergrad loan at six point five two percent, paid over the standard ten years.

lines.text: We use the standard loan formula. It blends principal and interest into one equal monthly payment.
lines.say: We use the standard loan formula. It blends principal and interest into one equal monthly payment.

lines.text: The answer: about $341 a month, every month, for 120 months.
lines.say: The answer: about three hundred forty-one dollars a month, every month, for a hundred twenty months.

lines.text: In month one, $163 of that payment is pure interest. That's almost half the payment.
lines.say: In month one, a hundred sixty-three dollars of that payment is pure interest. That's almost half the payment.

lines.text: The other $178 or so actually shrinks the loan. Over the years, that split slowly flips toward principal.
lines.say: The other hundred seventy-eight dollars or so actually shrinks the loan. Over the years, that split slowly flips toward principal.

lines.text: Over ten years, you'd pay back the $30,000 you borrowed, plus about $10,914 in interest.
lines.say: Over ten years, you'd pay back the thirty thousand dollars you borrowed, plus about ten thousand nine hundred fourteen dollars in interest.

lines.text: That's about $40,914 in total, or roughly 36% more than the original loan.
lines.say: That's about forty thousand nine hundred fourteen dollars in total, or roughly thirty-six percent more than the original loan.

lines.text: Now stretch the same loan to 20 years. The monthly payment drops to about $224.
lines.say: Now stretch the same loan to twenty years. The monthly payment drops to about two hundred twenty-four dollars.

lines.text: But total interest jumps to about $23,766. That's more than double. Lower payments, bigger total bill.
lines.say: But total interest jumps to about twenty-three thousand seven hundred sixty-six dollars. That's more than double. Lower payments, bigger total bill.

lines.text: Stretch that across 42.3 million borrowers, and you can see why the national total shrinks so slowly.
lines.say: Stretch that across forty-two point three million borrowers, and you can see why the national total shrinks so slowly.

lines.text: One fine-print note: federal loans charge simple daily interest, so real bills can differ a little from our math.
lines.say: One fine-print note: federal loans charge simple daily interest, so real bills can differ a little from our math.

lines.text: But the big lesson holds. With student loans, time is part of the price tag.
lines.say: But the big lesson holds. With student loans, time is part of the price tag.

lines.text: Chapter five: the pause, then new rules.
lines.say: Chapter five: the pause, then new rules.

lines.text: In March 2020, as the pandemic hit, federal student loan payments were paused, and the interest rate dropped to zero.
lines.say: In March twenty twenty, as the pandemic hit, federal student loan payments were paused, and the interest rate dropped to zero.

lines.text: That pause lasted about three and a half years. Interest restarted September 1, 2023, and bills came due from October.
lines.say: That pause lasted about three and a half years. Interest restarted September first, twenty twenty-three, and bills came due from October.

lines.text: With 0% interest for years, the national balance barely grew. That's the flat stretch on our chart.
lines.say: With zero percent interest for years, the national balance barely grew. That's the flat stretch on our chart.

lines.text: Since payments restarted, many borrowers have fallen behind. As of September 2026, 10.9% of student loan balances were 90+ days late.
lines.say: Since payments restarted, many borrowers have fallen behind. As of September twenty twenty-six, ten point nine percent of student loan balances were ninety or more days late.

lines.text: Federal data shows about 9.3 million borrowers in default as of June 2026, holding about $234 billion.
lines.say: Federal data shows about nine point three million borrowers in default as of June twenty twenty-six, holding about two hundred thirty-four billion dollars.

lines.text: Default isn't just a credit-score hit. By law, refunds and wages can be taken. Collections restarted in May 2025, then paused again in January 2026.
lines.say: Default isn't just a credit-score hit. By law, refunds and wages can be taken. Collections restarted in May twenty twenty-five, then paused again in January twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Repayment plans changed too. SAVE, an income-driven plan launched in 2023, ended in March 2026, when a court made a settlement final.
lines.say: Repayment plans changed too. SAVE, an income-driven plan launched in twenty twenty-three, ended in March twenty twenty-six, when a court made a settlement final.

lines.text: And on July 4, 2025, a big tax-and-spending law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, rewrote the loan rules.
lines.say: And on July fourth, twenty twenty-five, a big tax-and-spending law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, rewrote the loan rules.

lines.text: Most of its loan changes kicked in on July 1, 2026, for new borrowers.
lines.say: Most of its loan changes kicked in on July first, twenty twenty-six, for new borrowers.

lines.text: First, Grad PLUS is closed to new borrowers, apart from a limited phase-out for students already enrolled and borrowing.
lines.say: First, Grad PLUS is closed to new borrowers, apart from a limited phase-out for students already enrolled and borrowing.

lines.text: Graduate students now face a $20,500 yearly limit and a $100,000 total limit.
lines.say: Graduate students now face a twenty thousand five hundred dollar yearly limit and a one hundred thousand dollar total limit.

lines.text: Professional students, like future doctors and lawyers, get $50,000 a year and $200,000 total.
lines.say: Professional students, like future doctors and lawyers, get fifty thousand dollars a year and two hundred thousand total.

lines.text: Parent PLUS loans are now capped at $20,000 a year and $65,000 in total per student.
lines.say: Parent PLUS loans are now capped at twenty thousand dollars a year and sixty-five thousand in total per student.

lines.text: There's also a new lifetime limit of $257,500 in federal student loans, not counting Parent PLUS.
lines.say: There's also a new lifetime limit of two hundred fifty-seven thousand five hundred dollars in federal student loans, not counting Parent PLUS.

lines.text: Undergraduate limits didn't change. A dependent undergrad can still borrow up to $31,000 in total.
lines.say: Undergraduate limits didn't change. A dependent undergrad can still borrow up to thirty-one thousand dollars in total.

lines.text: Loans made since July 1, 2026 get two repayment choices: a tiered standard plan with fixed payments, or the new Repayment Assistance Plan, called RAP.
lines.say: Loans made since July first, twenty twenty-six get two repayment choices: a tiered standard plan with fixed payments, or the new Repayment Assistance Plan, called RAP.

lines.text: RAP charges 1 to 10% of adjusted gross income, at least $10 a month, and forgives what's left after 30 years of payments.
lines.say: RAP charges one to ten percent of adjusted gross income, at least ten dollars a month, and forgives what's left after thirty years of payments.

lines.text: RAP also waives unpaid monthly interest when payments are made on time, so balances don't balloon.
lines.say: RAP also waives unpaid monthly interest when payments are made on time, so balances don't balloon.

lines.text: Older loans can stay on older plans like IBR for now. Other legacy plans close by July 1, 2028.
lines.say: Older loans can stay on older plans like I B R for now. Other legacy plans close by July first, twenty twenty-eight.

lines.text: Supporters say caps could slow borrowing and pressure schools on price. Critics say some students may turn to private loans instead.
lines.say: Supporters say caps could slow borrowing and pressure schools on price. Critics say some students may turn to private loans instead.

lines.text: Either way, the $1.66 trillion already owed doesn't vanish. It still gets paid down one bill at a time.
lines.say: Either way, the one point six six trillion dollars already owed doesn't vanish. It still gets paid down one bill at a time.

lines.text: Chapter six: the recap.
lines.say: Chapter six: the recap.

lines.text: One: since 1965, Washington has backed student loans, and bankruptcy rules made them very hard to escape.
lines.say: One: since nineteen sixty-five, Washington has backed student loans, and bankruptcy rules made them very hard to escape.

lines.text: Two: after inflation, public college sticker prices about doubled in thirty years.
lines.say: Two: after inflation, public college sticker prices about doubled in thirty years.

lines.text: Three: Grad PLUS in 2006 and direct lending in 2010 made big loans easier to get.
lines.say: Three: Grad PLUS in twenty oh-six and direct lending in twenty ten made big loans easier to get.

lines.text: Four: interest over ten or twenty years can add a third or more to what was borrowed.
lines.say: Four: interest over ten or twenty years can add a third or more to what was borrowed.

lines.text: And that's how student debt reached $1.66 trillion, more than Americans owe on credit cards.
lines.say: And that's how student debt reached one point six six trillion dollars, more than Americans owe on credit cards.

lines.text: The one takeaway: every loan has two numbers that matter most, the rate and the time. Now you know how both work.

post.title: Student debt is bigger than credit card debt. Here's how it got to $1.66 trillion.
post.ig: Americans owe $1.66 trillion in student loans, more than on credit cards. Here's how it got so big.
post.tiktok: Student debt is bigger than all US credit card debt. Here's how it got to $1.66 trillion.
post.yt_desc:
As of the third quarter of 2026, Americans owed $1.66 trillion in student loans, more than the $1.29 trillion on credit cards, according to the New York Fed. This video explains how it got so big: the 1965 Higher Education Act and its bank guarantees, bankruptcy rules that made student loans hard to escape, a public college sticker price that about doubled after inflation from 1995-96 to 2025-26, and Grad PLUS and direct federal lending. College Board's newest figure puts 2026-27 in-state public four-year tuition and fees at $12,290. We run the math on a $30,000 loan at the 2026-27 rate of 6.52% (our math: about $10,914 in interest over 10 years), then walk through the 2020-2023 payment pause, the end of SAVE, and the 2025 law that changed loan limits and repayment plans from July 1, 2026.

CHAPTERS

Sources: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Household Debt and Credit Report (Q3 2026, Nov 2026; Q4 reports 2012-2024); Federal Reserve Board G.19 Consumer Credit via FRED; Federal Student Aid data center announcements (June 2026, Sept 2026) and 2026-27 interest rate announcement (June 2026); College Board, Trends in College Pricing and Student Aid 2025 and 2026; LBJ Presidential Library; Congressional Research Service reports on student loans in bankruptcy and the SAFRA Act; Public Law 119-21 (July 4, 2025) as summarized by the US Department of Education and university aid offices; US Department of Education (2023, 2025, 2026).

News and education, not financial advice.
